HOVER ANY MILESTONE FOR DETAIL

1956 · the name is coined

A summer workshop at Dartmouth College proposes that every aspect of learning could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. The three decades that follow are mostly hand-written rules and symbolic logic — clever, and brittle.

MACHINE LEARNING · stop writing the rules

Instead of coding every rule, you show the system labelled examples and it fits a statistical model. Backpropagation, decision trees, support vector machines. Progress now depends on data and compute rather than on the programmer’s patience.

DEEP LEARNING · 2012

AlexNet wins the ImageNet competition with a deep neural network trained on GPUs, and the error rate falls off a cliff. The layers learn their own features, so hand-crafted feature engineering fades away. Vision, then speech, fall within a few years.

2017 · the Transformer

“Attention Is All You Need” replaces sequential recurrence with self-attention, so a whole sequence trains in parallel. That is what makes scaling to billions of parameters economic — every model on this slide is a descendant of that paper.

GENERATIVE AI · 2020–2022

GPT-3 shows that scale alone buys general capability; ChatGPT puts it behind a chat box and reaches a mass audience in weeks. Diffusion models do the same for images. The machine now produces text, code and pictures instead of only classifying them.

HOVER EACH TERM

TOKEN · the unit

Models do not read words, they read tokens — chunks of characters. “The cat sat on the” is five of them, and the model’s entire job is to guess the next one. Roughly 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of an English word, and every API bills you per token, in and out.

TRAINING · the expensive part

The one-off build. The model reads an enormous amount of text and nudges billions of internal weights until its next-token guesses start matching reality. Weeks of GPU time and millions of dollars — the part you will almost certainly never do, and never need to.

INFERENCE · the cheap part

Running an already-trained model to get an answer. Every chat message and every API call is inference. This is the part you actually pay for, per token — and the part whose price has collapsed, which is what the next slide is about.

MODEL · the artefact

What training leaves behind: a large file of weights plus the code to run it. It is a component, not a monument — the same app can point at a frontier model today and a small local one tomorrow by changing a line of config.

REASONING · AGENTS · PHYSICAL AI · now

Three shifts at once: models that spend more compute thinking before they answer; agents that call tools, run code and work over many steps; and models wired into cameras, sensors and robots. The frontier moves from answering to doing.

The models are getting better. More importantly, the test is changing.

HOVER THE CHARTS FOR DETAIL

THE TEST · Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.1

An independent third party scores frontier models on ten evaluations and rolls them into one number; v4.1 (June 2026) deliberately re-weighted toward harder, more realistic agent work. The interesting part is not the ranking — it is what the field now thinks is worth measuring.

GENERAL KNOWLEDGE · 18%

AA-Omniscience Accuracy (8%), AA-LCR long-context reasoning (6%) and — the telling one — AA-Omniscience Non-Hallucination (4%), which gives credit for answering “I don’t know” instead of inventing something. Recall is now the smallest slice of the pie.

AGENTS · 34%

The largest slice, and the newest. GDPval-AA v2 (20%) scores long-horizon trajectories on economically valuable tasks; τ³-Bench Banking (14%) tests tool use and rule-following in a customer-service setting. Two years ago this category barely existed.

SCIENTIFIC REASONING · 24%

Humanity’s Last Exam (12%), GPQA (6%) and CritPt (6%): graduate-level and beyond physics, chemistry and biology, written specifically so they cannot be answered from memory. This is the slice that separates the frontier from the pack.

CODING · 24%

Terminal-Bench 2.1 (16%) — real tasks in a real terminal — plus SciCode (8%), writing scientific code from a research description. Note what both have in common: finish the job, not complete the snippet.

THE EFFICIENCY · Stanford AI Index 2025

The AI Index is Stanford HAI’s annual audit of the field. This chart tracks one narrow question: how small can a model get and still clear 60% on MMLU, a 57-subject multiple-choice exam? Holding the score fixed is what makes the comparison honest.

540B PARAMETERS · 2022

PaLM, Google’s flagship of the moment, needed 540 billion parameters to pass that 60% bar. Running it meant a cluster and a budget. Nobody was putting this in a classroom, let alone on a device in a field.

142× REDUCTION · in two years

Same bar, same exam, 142 times fewer parameters. The companion number from the same report: a GPT-3.5-equivalent query fell from about $20 per million tokens in Nov 2022 to about $0.07 by Oct 2024 — roughly 280×.

3.8B PARAMETERS · 2024

Microsoft’s Phi-3-mini cleared the same 60% bar with 3.8 billion parameters — small enough to run on a laptop, a phone, or the little board you will meet later in this deck. Capability stopped being something you rent by the hour.

1. FILES, TABS & EDITOR

Your whole project is just files. Tabs across the top, the one you are changing in the middle.

2. GIT & GITHUB

Every change is a checkpoint. Commit, then push — free undo, free backup, free history.

3. TERMINAL

Where git, Supabase and Vercel actually run — and where Claude Code and Codex do their work.

4. AI PAIR PANEL

Copilot, Claude Code, Codex. Describe the change, read the diff, decide what to keep.

5. SUPABASE + VERCEL

Database, auth and storage behind one URL — and a push that ends at a live link you can share.

COPILOT
Ask → generate → run → commit → push → live. The same loop, every time.
Start before you feel ready.
Micro-Example: “I want a page that records room temperature” → ask AI for architecture → create files in VS Code → run locally → save to Git → deploy → add sensor later
